CausalChain: Tumor cells produce EVs loaded with miR-155 and other modulators -> EVs are internalized by mature neutrophils -> EV cargo activates mTOR signaling in neutrophils -> mTOR activation drives metabolic reprogramming -> Neutrophils differentiate into granulocytic-MDSCs -> Granulocytic-MDSCs suppress T-cell activity and promote tumor progression
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that tumor-derived EVs, enriched with miR-155 and other modulators, initiate a cascade in mature neutrophils wherein EV uptake activates mTOR, driving metabolic reprogramming and conversion into immunosuppressive granulocytic-MDSCs. Critically, by employing temporally precise mTOR inhibition—augmented with real-time live-cell imaging and single-cell multi-omics to monitor neutrophil reprogramming—and by concurrently targeting detected compensatory signaling pathways, one can effectively block neutrophil conversion. This dual intervention will hinder the generation of granulocytic-MDSCs, thereby reducing tumor immune evasion and improving responses to immunotherapy.
Abstract: Tumor-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) deliver miR-155 and additional modulators that are hypothesized to initiate a signaling cascade in mature neutrophils, culminating in their conversion into immunosuppressive granulocytic-MDSCs. In this revised model, we propose that the EV cargo activates mTOR signaling, which triggers metabolic reprogramming and subsequent phenotypic conversion. However, rather than solely relying on mTOR inhibition, our approach integrates precise temporal control of mTOR activity with advanced monitoring techniques—including live-cell imaging, single-cell RNA sequencing, and CRISPR-based pathway interrogation—to identify and concurrently target compensatory signaling pathways. This integrative strategy aims to prevent the neutrophil-to–MDSC conversion, thereby reducing tumor-induced immune suppression and enhancing the efficacy of immunotherapeutic interventions.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis focused solely on inhibiting mTOR signaling during tumor EV uptake to prevent neutrophil conversion into immunosuppressive MDSCs. In the revised hypothesis, we have retained the causal chain from EV-mediated mTOR activation to neutrophil metabolic reprogramming and subsequent MDSC differentiation, but now explicitly incorporate advanced technological capabilities for temporal control and mechanistic dissection. By leveraging live-cell imaging, single-cell RNA sequencing, and CRISPR-based screening, the revised approach addresses potential compensatory pathways and optimizes therapeutic timing. This enhancement not only maintains the novelty and logical coherence of the original idea but also increases its practical implementability and robustness in targeting tumor immune evasion.
